summary:
Voronezh Oblast stands under the Russian national framework on gender identity and sexual orientation. The sources identify no Voronezh-specific deviation material enough to score separately, so the oblast is assessed at the Russian national score.

Parent framework. Russia presents severe legal and physical risks for transgender visitors, and the situation has deteriorated sharply since 2022. Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were banned outright in 2023, when the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents was signed. The Supreme Court has designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation, and the expanded propaganda law criminalises any public expression, including anything justifying gender transition. Foreigners who violate these laws face arrest, up to 15 days' detention and deportation, and official national government warnings explicitly tell LGBT travellers of this.

The current legal position is that same-sex sexual activity is not criminalised in Russia, but same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned, changes to gender markers on official documents are prohibited, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023.

The 2013 "gay propaganda" law is punishable by administrative fines of up to 400,000 rubles for individuals or detention of up to 15 days, with repeated offences escalating to criminal prosecution and up to four years' imprisonment. Since the November 2023 Supreme Court extremist designation, participation in the designated movement carries two to six years' imprisonment and organising it six to ten years under Article 282.2.

Enforcement is documented in volume. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions as of 30 June 2025, about 98 of them administrative and three criminal, for alleged participation in the international LGBT movement or displaying its symbols. Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges, among them three publishing-house staff charged in May 2025 under Article 282.2 who each face up to 12 years' imprisonment, and 81 people were found guilty in 98 administrative cases under Article 20.3 for displaying banned symbols.

Human Rights Watch records at least 139 people in Russia impacted by anti-LGBT laws between 2022 and 2024 and assesses that openly LGBT people are likely to face discriminatory treatment that, by its nature or repetition, may amount to persecution, the state being able but not willing to provide protection.

Physical coercion is documented. Within 48 hours of the Supreme Court ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, while at least two other venues were raided the same night. In December 2024 a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility. BBC Russian reported on 27 July 2024 that a transgender woman was lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found.
tangentialFactors:
The US State Department travel advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers. The UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (v2.0, June 2025, page updated 12 August 2026) affirms that LGBT people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims.

Enforcement is escalating in volume as well as severity. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under Russia's propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, and that fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget in the two years preceding.

Arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025, according to The Moscow Times on 23 June 2025, which reported a St Petersburg queer woman describing herself as "a second-class citizen" after the extremist designation. Human Rights Watch called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia.
localsOnly:
Russian residents face the full weight of the administrative and criminal codes. The administrative offence under Article 20.3 covers displaying banned symbols and has produced 98 guilty findings; the criminal offence under Article 282.2 covers participation in and organisation of the designated movement, with prison terms of two to six years for participants and six to ten years for organisers, and up to 12 years sought against the publishing-house staff charged in May 2025.

For residents, transition is closed off in practice as well as in law: gender-marker changes on official documents are prohibited, gender reassignment surgery has been barred since 2023, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned the same year. Same-sex sexual activity remains lawful, while same-sex marriage is banned.

Human Rights Watch recorded at least 139 people in Russia impacted by anti-LGBT laws between 2022 and 2024 and assesses that openly LGBT people are likely to face discriminatory treatment that, by its nature or repetition, may amount to persecution, the state being able but not willing to provide protection.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Voronezh Oblast specific enforcement data is sourced in this record. Whether oblast courts have issued convictions under Article 20.3 or Article 282.2, and whether any venues or individuals in Voronezh have been raided or detained on extremism or propaganda charges, is unresolved on the available material; the conviction figures cited are national totals.

The scope of documentation changes available to residents of Voronezh Oblast specifically, and the practice of local registry offices in refusing or granting gender-marker changes after the 2023 law, are not sourced here. The current status of the UK Home Office note cited above, whose page update date of 12 August 2026 postdates its June 2025 version, is also unresolved.
